items.prompt: State two social or economic objectives of government. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Governments pursue economic objectives such as employment, sustainable growth, price stability and a sustainable external economic position, alongside social aims such as improved living standards, fair opportunity, access to essential services and environmental protection. Objectives can conflict: a project creating employment may also damage a shared environment, while protection costs can limit some commercial activity. A business’s profit objective does not by itself show whether these wider aims are achieved. State the relevant outcome and parties rather than assume any increase in business output benefits everyone equally.
marking_guidance: Point: Governments pursue economic objectives such as employment, sustainable growth, price stability and a sustainable external economic position, alongside social aims such as improved living standards, fair opportunity, access to essential services and environmental protection.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.prompt: Explain why Omi’s effects on neighbours can justify intervention. Fictional Omi Blocks can increase profit by leaving costly dust control out while nearby residents bear cleaning inconvenience. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Government may intervene because business choices can affect people who do not participate in the transaction, because workers or consumers may need protection, because competition and information may be imperfect, or because access to essential services and development objectives may not be met by commercial incentives alone. Intervention can use rules, incentives, public provision or information. It also uses resources and can create compliance costs or unintended effects, so explain the problem and whether the measure addresses it. A private profit is not proof of social harm, and the existence of regulation is not proof it works. The decision shifts some consequences outside the firm’s own accounts, giving a reason to consider protection. A suitable response should reduce the stated dust rather than simply punish unrelated activity.
marking_guidance: Starting point: Government may intervene because business choices can affect people who do not participate in the transaction, because workers or consumers may need protection, because competition and information may be imperfect, or because access to essential services and development objectives may not be met by commercial incentives alone.

items.prompt: Define a social cost arising from a business decision. [2]
items.canonical_answer: A cost borne by the rest of society rather than by the business as a result of that decision; an external cost.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A cost borne by the rest of society rather than by the business as a result of that decision; an external cost.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: Cost-benefit analysis is the valuation by a government agency of social and private costs and benefits resulting from a decision. Here the treatment is descriptive: identify the likely positive and negative effects, who bears or receives them, alternatives and important uncertainties. A business profit forecast covers only part of that wider assessment. A severe lasting effect may matter even when another benefit is easier to count. Avoid pretending that a list of benefits on one side automatically outweighs fewer but more serious harms.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Cost-benefit analysis is the valuation by a government agency of social and private costs and benefits resulting from a decision.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.prompt: Explain how a descriptive appraisal should compare Hela’s realistic options. Fictional Hela Blocks compares operating without dust control, installing effective control or postponing the project. [6]
items.canonical_answer: A descriptive appraisal separates private business effects from external community effects and compares realistic choices. Explain the mechanism, who is affected, whether the effect is temporary or lasting and how protection could alter it. A clean production option may preserve output while reducing neighbours’ harm, although it costs resources. Evidence can be incomplete, so give a conditional judgement rather than invent precise values for unmeasured consequences. Benefits and costs can be distributed unevenly; a gain to the business does not automatically compensate a resident. Control can reduce residents’ dust inconvenience while allowing production, but adds a private cost. Compare whether it works and is affordable; postponement may avoid harm but forgo useful activity.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: A descriptive appraisal separates private business effects from external community effects and compares realistic choices.

items.prompt: Explain how Nela’s wider access benefit and noise cost could be addressed descriptively. Fictional Nela Workshop funds an access-road improvement that other residents can also use, while its deliveries add evening noise. [6]
items.canonical_answer: To apply the concepts, start with a stated decision and distinguish effects on the enterprise from effects on others. An external benefit is a gain to society beyond the business’s own return, such as other users gaining from a shared access improvement funded by a project. An external cost is harm or inconvenience borne by outsiders, such as disruption from deliveries. Describe alternatives and possible mitigation. A benefit elsewhere does not automatically remove a serious harm at the site; the resolution needs a reasoned balance and evidence. The wider access is an external benefit; neighbours’ noise is an external cost. Daytime delivery scheduling may preserve the useful access and business activity while reducing disturbance.

items.canonical_answer: In this syllabus, a social cost is a cost borne by the rest of society rather than the business because of a business decision, also called an external cost. It must identify an outsider’s consequence rather than relabel the firm’s own expenses. Describing the affected people makes the mechanism clear.

items.canonical_answer: Social benefits are the gains to society resulting from a business decision, also known as external benefits in the syllabus. Distinguish wider benefits from the enterprise’s private revenue. Shared infrastructure improvement can benefit other users without becoming their purchase from the firm. Identify who gains and why; do not assume every project provides the same external benefit.

items.prompt: Explain why pollution and finite-resource depletion need matching protection measures. A hypothetical producer discharges waste while another extracts a limited mineral resource. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Government can protect against pollution through standards, monitoring, enforcement, information and incentives for cleaner methods. It can protect non-renewable resources through extraction limits, conditions, conservation and incentives to use materials efficiently. The measure must affect the actual mechanism and be capable of implementation. A rule without monitoring may change little; an excessive or poorly targeted burden can create costs without proportionate benefit. Distinguish reducing ongoing emissions from conserving a finite resource stock. Planting trees does not replace extracted mineral deposits. Pollution controls address the discharge; extraction and conservation measures address depletion. Different problems need different measures rather than one generic environmental slogan.
marking_guidance: Starting point: Government can protect against pollution through standards, monitoring, enforcement, information and incentives for cleaner methods.

items.prompt: Explain how control standards and monitoring could reduce the workshop’s dust. A hypothetical workshop can contain its dust using a suitable maintained filter. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Pollution protection can set acceptable discharge or emission conditions, require effective control, monitor compliance and apply consequences or incentives. Explain how a measure changes behaviour or reduces the stated harm. Costs and practical enforcement matter. A charge may encourage reduction where a cleaner option exists, while a standard may be needed to secure a particular result. These are general policy options, not statements of a current legal rule or rate. A monitored dust-control condition targets the source. Merely publishing a rule without checking equipment performance would give weaker assurance.

items.prompt: Explain why an extraction limit addresses a different problem from pollution control. A hypothetical enterprise seeks to extract a finite local mineral deposit rapidly. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Non-renewable resources such as mineral deposits are finite on human time scales. Protection can limit extraction, require suitable use and restoration arrangements and encourage resource efficiency, recycling or alternatives. Restoration can reduce site damage but does not recreate the mineral stock already extracted. Balance current useful output against future availability and environmental consequences using the facts. Extraction conditions and efficiency measures can limit depletion and waste. A pollution filter alone would not decide how much of the stock is removed.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether effective dust control with monitoring is preferable to closing Tula immediately. Fictional Tula Bricks can install a proven effective dust filter at a manageable cost. Nearby households currently face dust disturbance. [8]
items.canonical_answer: Choose environmental protection by identifying the source, affected parties, severity, feasible alternatives and monitoring needs. A standard can require a result, an incentive can make cleaner methods more attractive and an extraction limit can constrain use of a finite stock. Compare effectiveness, cost and enforceability. Where a serious stated harm cannot be reduced adequately, restricting or postponing activity may be preferable to permitting it because it creates jobs. Where mitigation works, it may preserve useful production with less harm. Require effective control and monitoring rather than an unrelated measure or automatic closure. It directly addresses the harm while retaining output. The choice would change if the control could not prevent a severe stated effect.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: Choose environmental protection by identifying the source, affected parties, severity, feasible alternatives and monitoring needs.

items.prompt:
Fictional Hena Blocks proposes production near homes. It would create useful output and improve shared road access, but dust would inconvenience residents. Effective maintained dust control is available at a manageable cost. The choice is conditional approval with monitoring or refusing the project.

a(i) Define social cost in the syllabus sense. [2]
a(ii) State two possible environmental-protection measures. [2]
b State two effects on outsiders that could be social costs. [2]
c Explain how a descriptive appraisal should treat Hena’s road benefit and dust harm. [6]
d Evaluate conditional approval against refusal under the stated control facts. [8]
items.canonical_answer: a(i) A business-decision cost borne by the rest of society rather than the business, an external cost. a(ii) Monitored pollution standards and extraction limits. b Noise disturbance and dust-related inconvenience to neighbours. c Shared access can benefit other users while dust imposes a separate cost on residents. Include both alongside private production costs and benefits, examining severity, duration and control rather than treating profit as the whole appraisal. d Effective affordable control can preserve useful output and access while reducing the stated harm. Refusal avoids the project’s disturbance but also forgoes those benefits. Prefer conditional approval with verified maintenance and monitoring here; change the choice if protection proves inadequate rather than assume jobs excuse any harm.

items.prompt:
Fictional Hena Blocks proposes production near homes. It would create useful output and improve shared road access, but dust would inconvenience residents. Effective maintained dust control is available at a manageable cost. The choice is conditional approval with monitoring or refusing the project.

a Explain how Hena’s decision affects different parties and why its private profit alone cannot resolve the choice. [8]
b Evaluate monitored environmental conditions against refusing the project. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Owners assess private cost and return, users can gain shared road access and residents bear dust inconvenience. These are different recipients and burdens, so a business profit does not show that residents’ effects have disappeared or been compensated. A descriptive appraisal should examine the effective-control alternative and its ongoing requirements, as well as refusal. b The stated control can reduce harm at manageable cost, making conditional operation a way to retain benefits while protecting neighbours. Monitoring and maintenance use resources and must actually occur; an unenforced promise is insufficient. Refusal offers stronger avoidance of this activity but loses useful output and access. Choose conditions with performance verification under these facts, and restrict or stop activity if the required protection fails. The judgement depends on effective mitigation, not a numerical sum of unmeasured social effects.

items.prompt:
Fictional Omi Materials proposes a workshop with shared access improvements but noise affecting neighbours. An effective enclosure and daytime schedule can reduce the disturbance at a manageable cost. It compares monitored conditions with refusal.

Evaluate Omi’s controlled-operation option against refusal under the original facts. Give a concise descriptive plan. [12]
items.canonical_answer: Identify parties: business private return, other users’ access benefit and neighbours’ noise cost. Compare effective enclosure/daytime operation with refusal. Control preserves benefits but needs cost, maintenance and monitoring; refusal avoids this harm but loses the project benefits. Judgement: conditional operation while protection is effective. Do not count arguments as if their number establishes the balance or assume every effect has a precise money figure.

items.prompt:
Fictional Omi Materials proposes a workshop with shared access improvements but noise affecting neighbours. An effective enclosure and daytime schedule can reduce the disturbance at a manageable cost. It compares monitored conditions with refusal. For part (b) only, reliable assessment now shows the proposed controls cannot prevent a severe lasting harm to the nearby community. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate conditional operation at Omi under the original facts. [12]
b Evaluate the choice after the assessment of lasting harm changes. Explain whether the original judgement should hold. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a Affordable effective controls can reduce the stated disturbance and preserve shared access and useful activity. Require monitoring and review because a promise alone does not secure performance. Conditional operation is preferable to immediate refusal on the supplied facts. b The essential mitigation condition fails. Severe lasting harm cannot be dismissed because the business or road users gain. Refuse or postpone this proposal while investigating a genuinely safer site or method, rather than repeat ineffective conditions. The recommendation changes because the available protection no longer addresses the harm; keep the assessment descriptive and acknowledge what further evidence is needed.
